title: Spaza Shop Variables
description: Create variables for three items and calculate the total stock value.
starter_code:
bread = 15
milk = 18
chips = 12
total = bread + milk + chips
print("Total: R" + str(total))

hints: You need to store three numbers — what Python keyword creates a named value?
Try: bread = 15 — now do the same for milk and chips.
Add them: total = bread + milk + chips, then print('Total: R' + str(total))

checks.message: 💡 `total` should be a number — try adding your variables together.
💡 Your code runs but prints nothing — add a print() statement.

title: Taxi Fare Calculator
description: Calculate taxi fare based on distance and rate per km.
starter_code:
distance = 10
rate = 5
fare = distance * rate
print("Fare: R" + str(fare))

hints: You need a variable called `fare` — what calculation gives you the fare?
Fare = distance × rate. Try: fare = distance * rate
Now print it: print('Fare: R' + str(fare))

checks.message: 💡 `fare` should equal `distance × rate`. Check your formula.
💡 Print the fare!

title: Rainy Day Decisions
description: Use if-elif-else to decide what to do based on the weather.

hints: Start by creating a variable: weather = 'rainy'
Use `if` to check one condition, `elif` for another.
if weather == 'sunny': ... elif weather == 'rainy': ... else: ...

checks.message: 💡 You need both an `if` and an `elif` block.
💡 Your code runs but prints nothing — add print() inside each block.
💡 When weather is 'rainy' suggest staying inside.

title: Spaza Restocking Loops
description: Use a for loop to print a restocking message for every item.

hints: Create a list called `items` with some product names.
Use: items = ['Bread', 'Milk', 'Chips']
Then loop: for item in items:  print('Restocking ' + item)

checks.message: 💡 You need a `for` loop to go through each item.
💡 Your loop should print one line per item.

title: Super Functions
description: Define a function called `calculate_total` that takes a list of prices and returns their sum.
starter_code:
def calculate_total(prices):
    total = sum(prices)
    return total

prices = [15, 18, 12]
total_price = calculate_total(prices)
print("Total Price: R" + str(total_price))

hints: You need to define a function — start with `def`.
def calculate_total(prices):  — now add the body.
Inside the function: total = sum(prices)  then  return total

checks.message: 💡 Name your function exactly `calculate_total`.
💡 Check your sum() logic.

title: Super Spaza List Magic
description: Use list comprehensions to raise all prices by R3, and filter prices above R20.
starter_code:
prices = [12, 18, 25, 8, 30]
new_prices = [p + 3 for p in prices]
expensive = [p for p in prices if p > 20]
print(new_prices)
print(expensive)

hints: You need two lists: `new_prices` and `expensive`.
Use a list comprehension: [p + 3 for p in prices]
Filter expensive ones: [p for p in prices if p > 20]
You need two lists: `new_prices` and `expensive`.
Use a list comprehension: [p + 3 for p in prices]
Filter expensive ones: [p for p in prices if p > 20]

checks.message: 💡 `new_prices` should be a list — use a list comprehension.
💡 `new_prices` should add 3 to every price.

checks.message: 💡 `expensive` should only include prices above 20.

title: Spaza Inventory Dictionary
description: Store each item with its price in a dictionary, then work out the total value of the stock.

hints: A dictionary maps a name to a value, like {'Bread': 15}.
Try: inventory = {'Bread': 15, 'Milk': 18, 'Chips': 12}
Use inventory.values() to get just the prices.
You need a variable called `total_value`.
Add up the prices with sum(inventory.values())
total_value = sum(inventory.values())

checks.message: 💡 `total_value` should be the sum of every price in `inventory`.
💡 Print the total value!

title: Mini Project: Class Grade Book
description: Write a function that works out the class average from a dictionary of learner names and marks.

hints: Define a function: def class_average(grades):
Inside it, add up the marks and divide by how many there are.
return sum(grades.values()) / len(grades)

checks.message: 💡 Name your function exactly `class_average`.
💡 For {'A': 50, 'B': 100} the average should be 75. Check sum()/len().
